what: Walking-beam pumpjack. Walking-beam pump (pumpjack). Motor A turns a 16 mm crank. A 64 mm pitman joins the crank pin to one arm of a walking beam (48 mm from the beam pivot); the other arm (56 mm) carries a 64 mm pump rod that pushes a guided rack up and down like a pump plunger. Only the crank is driven; beam, rods and plunger are passive. No fluid is modelled. A crank-rocker four-bar nods a walking beam, and a 64 mm pump rod drives a guided rack as a pump plunger (no fluid is modelled). From the compiled lengths alone the loop predicts a 42.40° beam swing and a 40.58 mm stroke; the simulated beam follows it within 0.02°.
try: Open Solstice with its program, press Reset, then Run. The run takes about 55 s.
The first crank turn goes in four slow quarter-turn steps at 30°/s with a 3 s pause after each. At each pause, note the beam angle and the plunger height.
Then the crank turns back a full turn, forward a full turn and back again at 60°/s. Watch the beam reverse twice per crank turn and the plunger follow it.
Compare the two halves of the stroke: the beam does not swing up and down in equal crank angles, because the pitman is not perpendicular to the beam at both ends of its swing.
why: Crank, pitman, beam arm and the fixed distance between the crank axis and the beam pivot form a four-bar linkage. The crank is the shortest bar and Grashof's condition holds, so the crank turns all the way round while the beam only rocks (a crank-rocker). For each crank angle φ the loop closes where the pitman length fits: |B(β) − P(φ)| = 64 mm fixes the beam angle β. The far arm then moves the pump rod, and the rod length fixes the plunger height on its guide.
matters: Oil-field pumpjacks (nodding donkeys) and old mine pumps use exactly this layout: a fast, continuously turning crank becomes a slow, large up-and-down stroke at the well head. The same closed-loop calculation is used to size any four-bar linkage.
question: From the built lengths alone, how far does the beam swing and how long is the plunger stroke for one crank turn?
answer: Solving the loop over one crank turn gives a 42.40° beam swing and a 40.58 mm plunger stroke. The simulated beam follows the predicted angle within about 0.02° at every frame and the plunger within about 0.02 mm; the measured swing was 42.42° and the stroke 40.60 mm.
further: Change the crank radius on paper: a longer crank gives a larger swing until the four-bar no longer satisfies Grashof's condition, and then the crank can no longer turn all the way.
The ratio of the beam arms (56/48) scales the plunger motion relative to the pitman end; a real pumpjack uses it to trade force for stroke.
Removing the crank pin disconnects the linkage: the motor still turns a full revolution but the beam no longer follows the law. That is the causal control used to qualify this model.
Compare Rod Ratio, which compares two connecting-rod lengths, and Cross Ratio, another four-bar with a closed-form law.
formula: Crank r = 16 mm, pitman Lp = 64 mm, beam arms 48 mm and 56 mm (opposite sides), pump rod Lr = 64 mm. For crank angle φ: |B(β) − P(φ)| = Lp gives the beam angle β; |S − D(β)| = Lr with S on the plunger guide gives the plunger position. Over one turn: swing 42.40°, stroke 40.58 mm.
